lesson_title: From a Lump of Coal to Your Light Switch
hook_text: Two-thirds of the energy in the coal never reaches your home. Where does it go?
clip_script: Most of South Africa's electricity starts as coal from Mpumalanga. Coal stores chemical energy from plants that lived millions of years ago. At the power station it is crushed to powder and burned in a boiler, turning water into high-pressure steam. The steam blasts through a turbine, spinning it about 3 000 times a minute. The turbine turns a generator, where a giant magnet spins inside coils of copper wire, and that produces electricity. The steam is cooled in those curved towers, and the white cloud you see is water vapour, not smoke. But only about a third of the coal's energy becomes electricity. The rest is transferred to the surroundings as heat. And the chimneys release carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide and ash. That is the real cost behind the switch on your wall.
visual_style: Coal on a conveyor; flames in a boiler; steam spinning turbine blades; a magnet rotating in copper coils; cooling towers with white plumes; an energy bar shrinking to one third.
pacing: Question open, a rapid chain of stages, a pause on the efficiency number, a reflective close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and draw the energy chain from coal to light.
